gamedevelopment.title: Game Development
gamedevelopment.description: Build a small game from its core update loop through input, movement, collision, scoring, and a polished, tested finish.

modules.title: The Game Loop
modules.description: Understand how games repeatedly update their world and present the result.
notes: A game loop alternates between updating game state and rendering that state, repeating while the game is active.
Time-based updates use elapsed time (delta time) so motion can be expressed in units per second rather than per frame.
Keep state changes in the update step and make rendering a view of the current state; this separation makes behavior easier to test.
takeaways: A game loop repeatedly updates then renders.
Use elapsed seconds to make movement independent of frame rate.
Separate state updates from presentation.

modules.title: Coordinates and Input
modules.description: Represent positions consistently and translate player input into game actions.
notes: A 2D position is commonly represented by x and y values; choose a coordinate convention and apply it consistently.
Input handling should record intent, such as a direction or pressed action, for the update step to consume.
Decoupling input from movement lets the same movement rules work with keyboard, touch, or automated test input.
takeaways: Store a 2D position as a pair of coordinates.
Convert input into a clear action or direction.
Keep input collection separate from movement rules.

modules.title: Player Movement
modules.description: Move a character smoothly and keep it within the play area.
notes: Multiply speed by delta time when applying movement so a chosen speed has units such as pixels per second.
Normalize diagonal direction vectors when equal diagonal and straight-line speeds are desired; otherwise diagonals are faster.
Clamp positions to the play area's bounds to prevent a player from leaving the intended region.
takeaways: Scale movement by elapsed time.
Normalize direction when consistent diagonal speed matters.
Clamp coordinates to valid play-area bounds.

modules.title: Collision Detection
modules.description: Detect when simple game objects overlap and respond to the contact.
notes: For axis-aligned rectangles, overlap occurs when their horizontal and vertical intervals both intersect.
Use consistent rectangle dimensions and coordinate meanings, such as x and y for the top-left corner.
Collision detection identifies contact; a separate response decides what happens, such as stopping movement or collecting an item.
takeaways: Rectangle overlap requires intersection on both axes.
Use one consistent coordinate and size convention.
Keep collision detection distinct from its gameplay response.

modules.title: Score and Game State
modules.description: Track progress and represent transitions such as playing, winning, and losing.
notes: Keep score and status in explicit state rather than inferring them from display text.
Events such as collecting an item can update score and remove or mark the item as collected.
A small set of named states (for example, ready, playing, gameOver) makes allowed transitions easier to reason about.
takeaways: Represent score and status as explicit data.
Make one-time events idempotent to avoid duplicate rewards.
Name game states and manage their transitions deliberately.

modules.title: Polish and Testing
modules.description: Improve feedback, check edge cases, and make a small game reliable and pleasant to play.
notes: Clear feedback—such as a score change, brief animation, or restart prompt—helps players understand the result of an action.
Test boundary conditions including zero movement, maximum bounds, repeated collection, and game-over transitions.
Keep randomness controllable in tests by injecting values or a random-number function instead of relying on hidden global behavior.
A short playtest can reveal confusing controls and pacing issues that code-level checks do not catch.
takeaways: Test edge cases and game-state transitions, not only the happy path.
Give players clear feedback for important actions.
Playtest controls and pacing with real users when possible.

webdevelopment.title: Web Development
webdevelopment.description: Learn the foundations of building accessible, responsive web pages with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, forms, and practical debugging.

modules.title: HTML Structure
modules.description: Create meaningful page structure with semantic HTML elements.
notes: HTML describes a document's structure and meaning; semantic elements communicate the role of content to browsers and assistive technologies.
A document should include a doctype, language, character encoding, viewport metadata, and a descriptive title.
Use headings in a logical hierarchy and choose elements such as main, nav, article, and footer according to their purpose.
modules.code:
Trail Notes

Explore nearby paths.
modules.output: A page titled “Trail Notes” displays a main heading and the text “Explore nearby paths.”
takeaways: Use semantic elements to express content roles.
Include language, charset, viewport, and title metadata.
Keep heading levels meaningful and ordered.

modules.title: CSS Selectors and Layout
modules.description: Style elements with selectors and arrange content using modern layout tools.
notes: Selectors target elements by type, class, or relationship; classes are reusable hooks for styling groups of elements.
The cascade resolves competing declarations using origin, importance, specificity, and source order; avoid unnecessary specificity battles.
Flexbox is useful for one-dimensional alignment, while Grid is well suited to two-dimensional layouts.
The box model includes content, padding, border, and margin; box-sizing: border-box makes declared dimensions include padding and border.
modules.output: Elements with class card-list appear in a row with a 1rem gap; each card has padding and a border.
takeaways: Use classes for reusable styling and understandable selectors.
Choose Flexbox or Grid based on the layout's dimensional needs.
Understand how the box model affects element size.

modules.title: Responsive Design
modules.description: Adapt layouts to different viewport sizes with flexible sizing and media queries.
notes: Responsive layouts combine flexible widths, intrinsic content sizing, and breakpoints chosen when the design needs to change.
The viewport meta tag lets mobile browsers use the device width as the layout viewport.
Media queries apply styles conditionally; start with a usable narrow layout and enhance it for wider screens.
Images should scale within their containers to avoid overflowing the page.
modules.code:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<style>
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 1rem; }
@media (min-width: 700px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
</style>
modules.output: The grid shows one column below 700px and two equal columns at 700px or wider; images scale to fit their containers.
takeaways: Use flexible layouts before adding breakpoints.
Set the viewport for device-width rendering on mobile.
Use media queries to respond to content and viewport needs.

modules.title: JavaScript and the DOM
modules.description: Select page elements and update their content in response to user actions.
notes: The DOM is the browser's object representation of a document; JavaScript can query nodes and update their properties.
Use addEventListener to register behavior without embedding event-handler code in HTML attributes.
Prefer textContent for inserting plain text; assigning untrusted content to innerHTML can create cross-site scripting risks.
Check that a queried element exists when scripts may load before the relevant markup.
modules.code: 0
modules.output: Clicking Add changes the paragraph from 0 to 1, then increments it on each click.
takeaways: Use DOM queries to locate elements and event listeners to react to actions.
Update plain text with textContent rather than unsafe HTML insertion.
Ensure scripts run when the target elements are available.

modules.title: Forms and Accessibility
modules.description: Build forms that are understandable to assistive technologies and provide useful validation feedback.
notes: Associate each form control with a visible label using matching for and id values; placeholder text is not a replacement for a label.
Use appropriate input types and built-in constraints such as required and type=email to support user input and browser validation.
Group related controls with fieldset and legend when the group needs a shared label.
Validation should explain how to fix an error; do not rely on color alone to convey status.
modules.code:
<form>
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>
modules.output: A labeled email field and Subscribe button render; submitting an empty or invalid email is blocked by native browser validation.
takeaways: Connect visible labels to controls with for and id.
Use semantic input types and native constraints appropriately.
Make errors clear and actionable for all users.

modules.title: Shipping and Debugging
modules.description: Check a web page systematically, diagnose common issues, and prepare it for delivery.
notes: Use browser developer tools to inspect the DOM, computed styles, console errors, network requests, and responsive viewport behavior.
Validate HTML and test links, keyboard navigation, form behavior, and layouts at multiple viewport widths before shipping.
A production checklist should confirm correct asset paths, meaningful page metadata, and that no development-only errors remain.
Reproduce a bug, inspect the relevant evidence, make one focused change, and retest the affected behavior.
modules.output: Check complete (the assertion passes). In a browser, also verify the page at narrow and wide viewport widths.
takeaways: Use the console, inspector, and network panel to narrow down defects.
Test keyboard use, forms, links, and responsive layouts before delivery.
Retest after each focused fix and check for console errors.
